title: Which three numbers in a row are multiples of two, three and four?
description: Three numbers in a row must be a multiple of two, a multiple of three and a multiple of four, in that order. The video writes them as n, n plus one and n plus two, shows that n minus two is a multiple of twelve, and finds how often such sets occur.
teaching_notes: One idea: take a suitable number away from each of the three so that all three become the same expression, then use the smallest number all the divisors divide. Watch for students who stop at two, three and four and never ask whether there are more sets.

video_script.why: The student can take a common remainder away to get a multiple of both divisors and now does the same for three numbers in a row.
video_script.substitution: Write the numbers as n, n plus one and n plus two, take away two, three and four so each becomes n minus two, then use the smallest number two, three and four all divide.
video_script.anchor: three numbers in a row on a number strip, going up by one each time
video_script.payoff_line: A new set occurs every twelve numbers

final_answer.value: 2, 3, 4 and 14, 15, 16 and so on; a new set occurs every 12 numbers
final_answer.spoken: two, three, four and fourteen, fifteen, sixteen and so on, and a new set occurs every twelve numbers

hold_back: a new set occurs every 12 numbers
maths_rules: 2 is a multiple of 2, 3 is a multiple of 3, 4 is a multiple of 4
n is a multiple of 2, so n - 2 is a multiple of 2
n + 1 is a multiple of 3, so n + 1 - 3 = n - 2 is a multiple of 3
n + 2 is a multiple of 4, so n + 2 - 4 = n - 2 is a multiple of 4
n - 2 is a multiple of 12, so n = 12k + 2

<bookmark mark='two'/>With k as two, it is twenty six, twenty seven, twenty eight.
